column2: Clap a Beat, Draw a Picture
column5:
b1-arts-2: Claps a steady beat and sings simple songs
b1-arts-3: Draws a picture and talks about it
column9:
[text] Music has a steady BEAT, like your heartbeat: thump, thump, thump. 🥁

[text] Clap along to a song: clap, clap, clap!

[text] Drawing is another way to share ideas. ✏️ There's no wrong way to draw!

[tryit] Draw your favourite animal, then tell a grown-up all about it.

[parent] Ask 'Tell me about your picture' instead of 'What is it?'. Your child gets to explain their ideas.
column10:
Wikipedia: Beat (music) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(music) (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Drawing — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drawing (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-arts-1: Names primary colours and mixes two to make a new colour
column9:
[text] Red 🔴, yellow 🟡 and blue 🔵 are special paint colours.

[text] Mix them and you make NEW colours! 🎨

[text] Yellow + blue = green 🟢. Red + yellow = orange 🟠. Red + blue = purple 🟣.

[tryit] With a grown-up, mix two paint colours on paper. What did you make?

[parent] Washable paints or coloured water in clear cups work well. Let them predict first: 'What do you think will happen?'
column10: Wikipedia: Primary color — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_color (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-comp-1: Follows and gives simple step-by-step instructions (unplugged)
b1-comp-2: Knows machines follow instructions people give them
column9:
[text] Robots and computers follow steps, one at a time. 🤖

[text] The ORDER matters! Socks go on before shoes. 🧦👟

[text] If the steps are mixed up, things go wrong. Shoes then socks? Silly! 😄

[tryit] Be a robot! A grown-up gives you steps: 'Walk 2 steps. Turn around. Clap!'

[parent] Take turns being the 'robot' and the 'programmer'. Follow instructions very literally, so children see why clear steps matter.
column10: Wikipedia: Algorithm — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-dig-1: Asks a grown-up before using a screen or tapping something new
b1-dig-2: Knows screens have a time to stop
b1-dig-3: Tells a grown-up if something on a screen is scary or upsetting
column9:
[text] Tablets and phones can be fun! 📱

[text] Before you tap something new, ask a grown-up. 🙋

[text] If something makes you scared or sad, tell a grown-up right away. 💛

[text] Screens need a rest too. When time is up, we stop and play! ⚽

[parent] Keep devices in shared spaces and use them together at this age. Praise your child every time they come to you, so telling you becomes a habit.
column10: Wikipedia: Screen time — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screen_time (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-health-1: Washes hands properly and knows when (before eating, after toilet)
column9:
[text] Germs are tiny. Too tiny to see! 🦠

[text] Soap and water wash germs away. 🧼💧

[text] Rub, rub, rub! Fronts, backs and between fingers. Sing 'Happy Birthday' two times while you rub.

[tryit] Show a grown-up how you wash your hands.

[parent] Washing with soap for about 20 seconds (two rounds of 'Happy Birthday') helps remove germs. Key times: before eating, after the toilet, after playing outside and after touching animals.
column10:
WHO: World Hand Hygiene Day — https://www.who.int/campaigns/world-hand-hygiene-day (Reference only; text is original)
Wikipedia: Hand washing — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand_washing (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-health-5: Knows fruit and vegetables help us grow strong
column9:
[text] Fruit and vegetables help our bodies grow strong and stay well. 🥦🍎

[text] Eat the rainbow! Red tomatoes, orange carrots, green peas, purple grapes. 🌈

[text] Water helps too. 💧

[tryit] How many colours of fruit and vegetables can you eat today?

[parent] Offer new vegetables many times without pressure. Children often need to try a food 10+ times before they like it.
column10:
Wikipedia: Fruit — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fruit (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Vegetable — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vegetable (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-health-3: Knows the names of main body parts
b1-health-4: Knows their body belongs to them and to tell a trusted adult if something feels wrong
column9:
[text] Let's name body parts: head, shoulders, knees and toes! Eyes, ears, mouth and nose!

[text] Your body belongs to YOU. 💛

[text] If anyone touches you in a way that feels wrong, or asks you to keep a secret that feels bad, tell a grown-up you trust.

[text] You will never be in trouble for telling.

[parent] Use correct names for all body parts and agree on who your child's trusted adults are. Explain the difference between surprises (fun, shared soon) and secrets (never OK to keep about touching).
column10:
Wikipedia: Human body — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_body (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Child abuse prevention — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_abuse_prevention (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-health-2: Names basic feelings: happy, sad, angry, scared
column9:
[text] We all have feelings. 😊 happy, 😢 sad, 😠 angry, 😨 scared.

[text] All feelings are OK. It's what we DO with them that matters.

[text] When we feel big feelings, we can take a deep breath and tell a grown-up.

[tryit] Make a happy face, a sad face, then a surprised face in the mirror!

[parent] Name feelings out loud ('You look frustrated'). Children learn emotional words by hearing them in real moments.
column10: Wikipedia: Emotion — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotion (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-lang-2: Recognises the letters of their name and most capital letters
column9:
[text] Words are made of letters. There are 26 letters in the English alphabet: A to Z. 🔤

[text] Letters can be BIG (capital) like A, B, C, or small like a, b, c.

[text] Your name starts with a capital letter!

[tryit] Find the first letter of your name on a sign, a box or a book.

[parent] Magnetic letters, writing in sand or tracing letters with a finger help. Start with the letters in your child's name.
column10:
Wikipedia: Alphabet — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphabet (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Letter case — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letter_case (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-lang-3: Hears the first sound in a word (b-b-ball) and finds rhyming words
column9:
[text] Some words sound the same at the end. They RHYME! 🎵

[text] Cat 🐱 and hat 🎩 rhyme. Cat… hat… they both end with 'at'.

[tryit] Say these out loud: bee 🐝, tree 🌳, me! Do they rhyme?

[parent] Read the questions aloud. Stretch the ending sounds (c-AT, h-AT). Nursery rhymes and songs are a great way to practise rhyming every day.
column10: Wikipedia: Rhyme — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyme (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-lang-1: Listens to a short story and retells what happened in their own words
b1-lang-4: Holds a book the right way and knows print goes left to right
b1-lang-5: Uses new words learned from stories when talking
column9:
[text] We hold a book the right way up. 📖 We start at the front cover.

[text] We read words from left to right ➡️, and turn pages one at a time.

[text] After a story, we can tell it again: what happened first, next and at the end?

[text] Stories teach us new words. Try using a new word today!

[parent] Read together daily. Ask 'What happened next?' and 'How did they feel?'. Let your child turn the pages and point to words as you read.
column10:
Wikipedia: Storytelling — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storytelling (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Book — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-math-4: Compares: more/less, bigger/smaller, longer/shorter
b1-math-5: Continues a simple pattern (red, blue, red, blue…)
column9:
[text] An elephant is BIGGER than a mouse. A mouse is SMALLER. 🐘🐭

[text] A long snake 🐍 and a short worm 🪱. Long and short!

[text] A PATTERN repeats: 🍎🍌🍎🍌🍎… What comes next? 🍌!

[tryit] Make a pattern with spoons and forks, or two colours of blocks.

[parent] Use words like more, fewer, longer and taller in daily life. Clapping patterns (clap, clap, stamp) also count!
column10: Wikipedia: Pattern — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pattern (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-math-1: Counts objects up to 10, one number for each object
b1-math-2: Recognises numerals 0–10
column9:
[text] Hold up one finger. ☝️ That is ONE.

[text] Let's count together: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5! 🖐️ Five fingers on one hand.

[tryit] Find 5 toys. Touch each one and count out loud.

[parent] Point to each object as your child counts so they match one number to one object. If they skip, gently start again together — no rush.
column10: Wikipedia: Counting — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counting (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-math-3: Names circle, square, triangle and rectangle in everyday things
column9:
[text] A CIRCLE is round, like a plate. ⚪

[text] A SQUARE has 4 straight sides, all the same. 🟦

[text] A TRIANGLE has 3 sides and 3 corners. 🔺

[text] A RECTANGLE has 4 sides, two long and two short, like a door. 🚪

[tryit] Go on a shape hunt! Find a circle, a square and a triangle at home.

[parent] Name shapes in everyday things: wheels, windows, sandwiches cut in halves. Counting corners together builds early math.
column10: Wikipedia: Shape — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shape (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-money-3: Helps with simple chores: tidy toys, put clothes away
column9:
[text] Everyone in a family can help! 🏠

[text] You can tidy your toys, put clothes in the basket and help set the table.

[text] Helping makes you feel proud and big! 💪

[tryit] Choose one job to do today, like putting your shoes away.

[parent] Small, regular jobs build responsibility. Praise effort, not perfection.
column10: Wikipedia: Housekeeping — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Housekeeping (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-money-1: Knows we use money to buy things
b1-money-2: Understands waiting and saving (sometimes we wait to get something)
column9:
[text] We use money to buy things. 🪙

[text] Sometimes we don't spend it. We SAVE it in a jar. 🫙

[text] Little by little, the jar fills up. Then we can buy something special! ⭐

[tryit] Find a jar. Draw a picture of something you'd like to save for and stick it on.

[parent] A clear jar lets children SEE savings grow. Small coins, regularly, teach patience better than big amounts once.
column10: Wikipedia: Saving — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saving (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-sci-1: Names the five senses and what each one does
column9:
[text] We learn about the world with our five senses! 🌍

[text] We SEE with our eyes. 👀 We HEAR with our ears. 👂

[text] We SMELL with our nose. 👃 We TASTE with our tongue. 👅

[text] We TOUCH and feel with our skin, like our fingers. ✋

[tryit] Close your eyes. What can you hear right now?

[parent] Play 'I spy' and 'what's that sound?'. Name the sense each time: 'You used your ears!'. Never ask a child to taste unknown things to test their senses.
column10: Wikipedia: Sense — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-sci-4: Sorts things: floats/sinks, hard/soft, hot/cold
column9:
[text] Some things FLOAT on water. Some things SINK to the bottom. 💧

[text] A leaf and a plastic duck float. 🦆🍃 A stone and a coin sink. 🪨🪙

[text] We can also sort things: hard or soft, hot or cold.

[tryit] With a grown-up, fill a bowl with water. Guess first: float or sink? Then test!

[parent] Always supervise water play. Ask 'What do you think will happen?' before each test. Guessing first is real science!
column10: Wikipedia: Buoyancy — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buoyancy (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-sci-2: Knows living things need food, water and air
b1-sci-3: Notices weather and the four seasons (or wet/dry seasons)
column9:
[text] Living things grow and need food, water and air. 🌱🐶👧

[text] A rock doesn't eat or grow. It is not alive. 🪨

[text] Weather changes: sunny ☀️, rainy 🌧️, windy 💨, snowy ❄️.

[text] Many places have four seasons: spring, summer, autumn and winter. Some places have a wet season and a dry season.

[parent] Look out of the window each day and name the weather together. Plant a seed in a cup and water it to watch something living grow.
column10:
Wikipedia: Life — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Season — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Season (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-think-3: Puts 3 pictures of a story in order (first, next, last)
b1-think-4: Asks 'why?' and 'what if?' questions
column9:
[text] Stories happen in order: FIRST, NEXT, LAST.

[text] Planting a seed: first dig a hole 🕳️, next put in the seed 🌰, last water it 💧.

[text] Good thinkers ask 'Why?' and 'What if?' 🤔 Like: Why is the sky blue? What if it rained jelly?

[tryit] Tell someone three things you did today, in order: first, next, last.

[parent] Welcome 'why' questions, even the tricky ones. 'I don't know, let's find out together' is a great answer.
column10:
Wikipedia: Sequence — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sequence (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Curiosity — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curiosity (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-think-1: Sorts objects by colour, shape or size
b1-think-2: Spots what is different / the odd one out
column9:
[text] Let's be detectives! 🔍

[text] Look: 🍎 🍌 🍇 🚗

[text] Three are fruits. The car is different. The car is the ODD ONE OUT! 🚗

[tryit] Put your toys in groups: things that are red, things that are soft, things with wheels.

[parent] Ask 'why?' after each answer. There can be more than one good answer, and explaining is the real skill.
column10: Wikipedia: Categorization — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Categorization (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b1-world-2: Knows the difference between day and night, today, yesterday and tomorrow
b1-world-3: Knows people around the world speak different languages, eat different food and wear different clothes — and that is good
column9:
[text] In the DAY the Sun is in the sky. ☀️ At NIGHT it's dark and we can see the Moon and stars. 🌙⭐

[text] Yesterday was before today. Tomorrow comes after today.

[text] People around the world speak different languages! 'Hello' can be 'Hola', 'Namaste', 'Bonjour' or 'Ni hao'. 🌍

[text] Different is good. We can learn from each other!

[parent] Use 'yesterday / today / tomorrow' at bedtime. If your family speaks more than one language, celebrate it!
column10:

Wikipedia: Language — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Language (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b1-world-4: Celebrations and festivals from many cultures
column9:
[text] All around the world, families celebrate special days called festivals. 🎉

[text] Diwali has little lamps 🪔. Eid often has new clothes and sharing sweets. Christmas has decorated trees 🎄. Lunar New Year has red lanterns 🏮.

[text] Some festivals are religious and some are not. People celebrate in many different ways.

[text] When a friend tells you about their festival, listen and say 'That sounds lovely!'

[parent] Share your own family's celebrations, and talk kindly about others'. This lesson is descriptive only and is shown only if you unlock it.

column5: b1-world-1: Talks about their family and the people who help in their community
column9:
[text] Many people help us every day. 💛

[text] Doctors and nurses help us when we are sick. 🩺

[text] Firefighters put out fires and keep us safe. 🚒

[text] Farmers grow the food we eat. 🌾 Teachers help us learn. 📚

[tryit] Who helped you today? Say thank you to them!

[parent] Talk about helpers your child meets: bus drivers, shopkeepers, cleaners, grandparents. If you're comfortable, explain who to go to if they ever get lost (a police officer, or a parent with children).

column2: Lines, Shapes and Art Around the World
column5:
b2-arts-1: Uses line, shape, colour and texture in their own art
b2-arts-3: Looks at art and music from different cultures and says what they notice
column9:
[text] Artists use LINE (straight, wavy, zigzag), SHAPE, COLOUR and TEXTURE (how something feels: rough, smooth, bumpy).

[text] Art from around the world looks different: Aboriginal dot paintings from Australia, Madhubani art from India, Mexican papel picado paper banners.

[text] When you look at art, say what you NOTICE: colours, shapes, how it makes you feel.

[tryit] Draw a picture using only wavy lines, then one using only dots!

[parent] Look at art from your family's heritage together, and from a culture you don't know yet.
column10:
Wikipedia: Elements of art — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elements_of_art (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Folk art — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_art (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b2-arts-2: Recognises loud/quiet, fast/slow and high/low in music
column9:
[text] Music can be loud or quiet. How loud music is, is called its DYNAMICS. 🔊🔈

[text] Music can be fast or slow. How fast music is, is called its TEMPO. 🐇🐢

[text] A lullaby is usually quiet and slow. A party song is often loud and fast!

[text] Musicians change dynamics and tempo to show feelings: calm, happy, scary or exciting.

[tryit] Clap a beat. Make it slow like a turtle, then fast like a rabbit. Now clap very quietly!

[parent] Free tools like Chrome Music Lab let children play with tempo. Ask how different music makes them feel.
column10:
Wikipedia: Dynamics (music) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamics_(music) (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Tempo — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b2-comp-1: Writes an algorithm (step-by-step instructions) for an everyday task
b2-comp-3: Finds and fixes a bug in a short set of instructions (debugging)
column9:
[text] An ALGORITHM is a list of steps to do a job, like a recipe.

[text] Computers follow algorithms exactly. They can't guess what we mean!

[text] A mistake in the steps is called a BUG. 🐞 Finding and fixing it is called DEBUGGING.

[text] Example: 'Brush teeth: 1. Rinse. 2. Brush. 3. Put toothpaste on brush.' The bug: step 3 should come before step 2!

[tryit] Write an algorithm for making a glass of water. Ask someone to follow it exactly. Any bugs?

[parent] Following instructions literally ('you said pick up the cup, not fill it!') makes this lesson memorable and funny.
column10:
Wikipedia: Algorithm — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Debugging — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debugging (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b2-comp-2: Makes a character move with block code (sequence)
column9:
[text] Block code lets you build programs by snapping blocks together, like LEGO for computers. 🧱

[text] A SEQUENCE is blocks in order: 'move 10 steps' → 'turn right' → 'say Hello!'

[text] The computer runs the blocks from top to bottom, one at a time.

[tryit] Try a free block-coding app (like ScratchJr) with a grown-up. Make a character walk and wave!

[parent] ScratchJr and Code.org are free. Let your child explain their program to you. That's great learning.
column10:
Wikipedia: Visual programming language — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_programming_language (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Scratch (programming language) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scratch_(programming_language) (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5:
b2-dig-1: Knows what personal information is (name, address, school, photos) and keeps it private
b2-dig-2: Knows people online may not be who they say they are
column9:
[text] Some things about you are PRIVATE. That means just for you and your family. 🔒

[text] Private things are: your full name, home address, phone number, school, passwords and photos of you.

[text] Online, people may not be who they say they are. A 'kid' online could really be a grown-up.

[text] If anyone online asks for private things, stop. Tell a grown-up you trust.

[parent] Agree on simple family rules: never share private details online, and always tell a parent if someone asks. Praise your child for telling you, even if they already shared something.
column10: Wikipedia: Personal data — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_data (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column2: Is It True? And What Is AI?
column5:
b2-dig-3: Knows not everything online is true
b2-dig-4: Knows AI helpers are computer programs, not people, and can make mistakes
column9:
[text] Not everything online is true. Anyone can post anything!

[text] Ask: Who made this? Does it sound too amazing? Can a grown-up check it in a trusted place?

[text] AI helpers, like Hoot, are computer programs, not people. They don't have feelings, and they can make mistakes.

[text] If an AI says something that seems wrong or upsetting, tell a grown-up.

[parent] Look at a silly fake photo online together and talk about how you can tell it's not real.
column10:
Wikipedia: Misinformation — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misinformation (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Chatbot — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatbot (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b2-health-1: Knows the food groups and what a balanced plate looks like
column9:
[text] Food gives your body energy to grow, play and think.

[text] A balanced plate has lots of fruit and vegetables. About half the plate! 🥕🍎

[text] It also has grains like rice, bread or roti 🍚, and protein like beans, eggs, fish or meat 🥚.

[text] Water is the best drink. Sweets and fizzy drinks are 'sometimes' foods.

[tryit] Draw your dinner plate. Is half of it fruit and vegetables?

[parent] Families eat in many ways (vegetarian, halal, kosher and more). Every way can be balanced. Avoid calling foods 'bad'; 'sometimes foods' is kinder and more accurate.
column10:
WHO: Healthy diet fact sheet — https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/healthy-diet (Reference only; text is original)
Wikipedia: Healthy diet — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthy_diet (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b2-health-4: Knows safe/unsafe touch, safe and unsafe secrets, and who their trusted adults are
column9:
[text] Your body belongs to you. Private parts are the parts covered by a swimsuit.

[text] Safe touch feels OK, like a high five or a hug you want. Unsafe touch feels wrong or confusing. You can say NO.

[text] SURPRISES are fun and get told soon (a birthday present). SECRETS that make you feel worried should be told to a trusted adult.

[text] Make a list of 3 trusted adults you can tell anything. If one doesn't listen, tell another.

[parent] Use correct names for body parts. Reassure your child they will never be in trouble for telling you something. Many organisations publish free guides on 'body safety' conversations.
column10:
Wikipedia: Child abuse prevention — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_abuse_prevention (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))
Wikipedia: Personal boundaries — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_boundaries (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b2-health-3: Names more feelings and simple calm-down strategies (breathing, counting)
column9:
[text] Feelings have names: excited, nervous, frustrated, jealous, proud, lonely.

[text] Naming a feeling helps it shrink: 'I feel frustrated because my drawing went wrong.'

[text] Calm-down tools: smell the flower, blow the candle (slow breaths), count to 10, squeeze a pillow, ask for a hug.

[tryit] Practise 'flower and candle' breathing: breathe in through your nose like smelling a flower, then blow out slowly like a candle.

[parent] Practise calm-down tools when your child is calm, so they're easier to use when upset.
column10: Wikipedia: Emotional self-regulation — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emotional_self-regulation (CC BY-SA 4.0 (reference; text is original))

column5: b2-health-2: Knows why sleep, exercise and brushing teeth matter
column9:
[text] Children your age need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep. Sleep helps you grow and remember what you learned.

[text] Moving your body every day keeps your heart and muscles strong. Run, dance, jump, play!

[text] Brush your teeth twice a day, for about 2 minutes, to keep them healthy. 🪥

[tryit] Make a chart: did you sleep well, play actively and brush twice today?

column9:
[text] FICTION books are made-up stories, like a dragon who bakes cakes. 🐉

[text] NON-FICTION books give real facts, like a book about how volcanoes work. 🌋

[text] Non-fiction often has headings, photos, labels and a contents page.

column5: b2-lang-3: Writes simple sentences with a capital letter and full stop
column9:
[text] A sentence is a group of words that makes sense on its own.

[text] Every sentence starts with a CAPITAL letter.

[text] A telling sentence ends with a full stop (.). Example: The cat is asleep.

[text] An asking sentence ends with a question mark (?). Example: Where is my hat?

[text] An exciting sentence can end with an exclamation mark (!). Example: We won!

[tryit] Write one telling sentence, one asking sentence and one exciting sentence about your day.

[parent] Read your child's sentences aloud with expression. They can hear the difference between '.', '?' and '!'.

column9:
[text] Letters make sounds. To read a new word, say each sound and blend them: c-a-t → cat!

[text] Some letters team up: 'sh' in ship, 'ch' in chip, 'th' in thin.

[text] Some words are tricky and don't follow the rules, like 'the', 'said' and 'was'. We learn these by sight.

[tryit] Sound out: d-o-g, f-i-sh, s-u-n. What words did you make?

[parent] Point under each sound as your child blends. Short, daily practice (5–10 minutes) beats long sessions.

column9:
[text] After reading, ask: WHO is in the story? WHAT happened? WHERE did it happen?

[text] Stuck on a new word? Look for clues in the picture and the sentence around it.

[fact] Example: 'The enormous elephant was so big it could hardly fit through the gate.' 'So big' tells you enormous means very big!

column2: Adding Big Numbers with Tens and Ones
column5:
b2-math-2: Adds and subtracts within 100, including word problems (GPF G2–3)
b2-math-1: Reads, writes and compares numbers to 1,000; understands place value (hundreds, tens, ones)
column9:
[text] The number 23 has 2 tens and 3 ones.

[text] To add 23 + 15, add the tens first. 2 tens + 1 ten = 3 tens. That is 30.

[text] Then add the ones. 3 + 5 = 8. So 30 + 8 = 38!

[tryit] Use bundles of 10 sticks and loose sticks to show 23 + 15.

[parent] Ask your child to say how many tens and ones are in each number before adding. Real objects (sticks, coins, blocks) make it concrete.

column5: b2-math-6: Understands halves and quarters of a shape
column9:
[text] A HALF means 2 EQUAL parts. We write it ½.

[text] A QUARTER means 4 EQUAL parts. We write one quarter ¼.

[text] The parts must be the same size. Otherwise they aren't halves or quarters!

[tryit] Fold a paper square in half, then in half again. How many equal parts now?

[parent] Share snacks fairly: 'Let's cut it in half so we each get the same.'

[text] A PICTURE GRAPH uses pictures to show numbers. If each 🍎 means 1 child, 4 🍎 means 4 children.

[text] Look at the title and the key to understand a graph.

[tryit] Measure your pencil, your hand and a spoon with a ruler. Which is longest?

[parent] Let your child measure real things. Line the object up with 0, not with the end of the ruler!

column5: b2-math-4: Tells time to the hour and half hour; recognises coins and notes
column9:
[text] On a clock, the short hand shows the hour. The long hand shows the minutes.

[text] When the long hand points to 12, it's 'o'clock'. When it points to 6, it's 'half past'.

[text] We count money by adding coins and notes. If something costs less than you pay, you get CHANGE back.

[fact] Example: a toy costs 7. You pay 10. Your change is 10 − 7 = 3.

[parent] Use your local coins for shop role-play. Ask your child to read the clock at key times (lunch, bedtime).

column5: b2-math-3: Understands multiplication as equal groups; knows 2, 5 and 10 times tables
column9:
[text] Multiplication means equal groups. 3 groups of 2 apples = 2 + 2 + 2 = 6. We write 3 × 2 = 6.

[text] The 2 times table counts in 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10…

[text] The 5 times table counts in 5s: 5, 10, 15, 20… The 10 times table counts in 10s: 10, 20, 30…

[fact] 3 × 2 is the same as 2 × 3. You can swap the numbers!

[parent] Count in 2s, 5s and 10s on walks or stairs. Real objects (coins, socks in pairs) make it concrete.

b2-money-4: Life skills: pack own school bag, tie shoelaces, simple tidy routines
b2-money-1: Counts money and gives change in simple cases
column9:
[text] Growing up means learning to do things yourself: packing your school bag, tying shoelaces, getting dressed.

[text] A checklist helps: lunchbox, water bottle, homework, coat. Tick them off! ✅

[text] Shoelaces: cross the laces, tuck one under, pull tight, make 'bunny ears' and cross them over!

[tryit] Make a checklist for your school bag and stick it by the door.

[parent] Give extra time in the morning so your child can practise. Doing it themselves, slowly, builds confidence.

b2-money-2: Understands needs vs wants
b2-money-3: Understands saving for a goal (a savings jar)
column9:
[text] A NEED is something we must have to live and be safe: food, water, a home, clothes.

[text] A WANT is something nice to have, but we can live without it: toys, sweets, games.

[text] Families pay for needs first. Then, if there's money left, some wants.

[text] Saving helps you get a want later. Put a little money aside each week.

[tryit] Make two lists: 3 needs and 3 wants. Which want would you save for?

[parent] Share a simple real example, like choosing between two snacks at the shop. Children learn a lot from seeing choices made out loud.

column9:
[text] MAMMALS have hair or fur and feed their babies milk (dogs, whales, humans).

[text] BIRDS have feathers and lay eggs. FISH live in water and breathe with gills. INSECTS have 6 legs.

[text] A HABITAT is an animal's home: ocean, desert, forest, polar ice…

[fact] A whale is a mammal, not a fish! It breathes air and feeds its babies milk.

[parent] Sort toy animals into groups together, and talk about why. Explaining 'why' matters more than the answer.

column5: b2-sci-4: Knows the Sun, Earth and Moon and why we have day and night
column9:
[text] The Earth spins around like a top. It takes one day (24 hours) to spin once.

[text] When your side faces the Sun, it's DAY. When it faces away, it's NIGHT.

[text] The Earth travels around the Sun. One trip takes a year. The Moon travels around the Earth.

[fact] The Sun is a star, the closest one to us!

[parent] In a dark room, use a torch as the Sun and a ball as the Earth. Spin the ball slowly to show day and night.

column5: b2-sci-5: Makes a prediction and does a simple fair test
column9:
[text] Scientists PREDICT (make a smart guess), then TEST to find out.

[text] A fair test changes only ONE thing. Everything else stays the same.

[fact] Example: Which ball bounces highest? Drop each from the SAME height onto the SAME floor. Only the ball changes.

[tryit] Predict which paper aeroplane design flies furthest. Throw each the same way and measure!

[parent] Ask 'What do you think will happen?' before every experiment. It's fine to be wrong. That's how science works!

column9:
[text] Plants need sunlight ☀️, water 💧, air and soil (or nutrients) to grow.

[text] ROOTS take in water. The STEM holds the plant up. LEAVES make food using sunlight. FLOWERS make seeds.

[fact] Plants make their own food from sunlight, air and water. This is called photosynthesis.

[tryit] Put a bean in a wet tissue in a clear cup. Watch the roots grow over a week!

[parent] A windowsill seed is a great science project. Ask what would happen with no water or no light, then test it.

column5: b2-sci-3: Knows the states of matter: solid, liquid, gas
column9:
[text] Everything around us is made of matter. Matter can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.

[text] A SOLID keeps its shape. A rock, a spoon and ice are solids. 🧊

[text] A LIQUID flows and takes the shape of its cup. Water and juice are liquids. 💧

[text] A GAS spreads out to fill any space. The air we breathe is a gas. 🎈

[fact] Water can be all three! Ice (solid), water (liquid) and steam (gas).

[tryit] With a grown-up: put an ice cube on a plate. Check it every 10 minutes. What happens?

[parent] Supervise any activity with hot water or steam. Ask 'does it keep its shape?' to help your child sort things.

column5: b2-think-2: Tells fact from opinion in simple sentences
column9:
[text] A FACT is something we can check and prove is true. 'A week has seven days.'

[text] An OPINION is what someone thinks or feels. 'Mondays are boring.' Others may disagree!

[text] Clue words for opinions: best, worst, beautiful, boring, I think, I feel.

[text] Opinions are fine to have. But it's good to know when something is an opinion.

[tryit] Say one fact and one opinion about your favourite animal.

[parent] Model it during the day: 'That's my opinion, you might disagree!' This builds respect for different views.

[text] Logic puzzles need careful thinking. Explain HOW you solved it, not just the answer.

[text] Mistakes help your brain grow! When something is hard, say 'I can't do it YET.'

column5: b2-world-1: Names the 7 continents and 5 oceans and finds them on a map/globe
column9:
[text] Earth's land is split into big pieces called continents. Most maps show seven.

[text] The seven continents are: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia (part of Oceania), Europe, North America and South America.

[fact] Some countries teach six continents, joining North and South America, or Europe and Asia. Both ways are OK!

[text] Asia is the biggest continent. Antarctica is the coldest. Almost nobody lives there all year.

[text] The five oceans are: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. The Pacific is the biggest.

[tryit] Find your continent on a map or globe. Which ocean is closest to you?

[parent] A cheap globe or a free online map makes this concrete. Find where family or friends live.

b2-world-4: Learns about children's lives in different countries

[text] Long ago, there were no phones or computers. Children wrote letters and played outside with simple toys.

[text] Today, children around the world live in many ways: some walk far to school, some live in cities, some on farms, some by the sea.

[text] Kids everywhere like to play, learn and spend time with family. We're more alike than different!

[text] The KEY shows what the symbols mean: a blue line might be a river, a tree symbol might be a park.

[text] The compass shows directions: North (up), South (down), East (right) and West (left).

[fact] A way to remember: 'Never Eat Soggy Waffles' goes clockwise: North, East, South, West.

[text] Some of the biggest religions are Christianity, Islam, Hinduism and Buddhism. There are many others, like Sikhism and Judaism.

[text] Each has special places (churches, mosques, temples, gurdwaras, synagogues), special books and festivals.

[text] Many people aren't religious and find meaning in other ways. Everyone deserves respect.

[text] You can sort instruments by how they make sound: plucked or bowed strings, blowing air, or hitting.

[text] Artists arrange colours on a circle called a COLOUR WHEEL.

[text] WARM colours are reds, oranges and yellows. They can feel energetic, sunny or fiery.

[text] COOL colours are blues, greens and purples. They can feel calm, peaceful or cold.

[text] COMPLEMENTARY colours sit opposite each other on the wheel, like blue and orange. Side by side, they make each other 'pop'.

[fact] Artists use warm and cool colours to create mood. A painting of a cosy fire uses warm colours. A winter night uses cool ones.

[tryit] Draw the same tree twice: once in warm colours and once in cool colours. How does each one feel?

[text] The internet is a giant network of computers connected by cables, Wi-Fi, phone signals and even undersea cables.

[text] When you send a message, it's split into small PACKETS. They travel separately and are put back together at the other end.

[text] Each device has an address (an IP address) so packets know where to go, a bit like a postal address.

[fact] Most internet data between continents travels through cables under the ocean, not through satellites.

[text] A CONDITION (if-then) makes a decision. 'IF it is raining THEN take an umbrella, ELSE wear sunglasses.'

[text] Games use both! 'Repeat forever: IF touching a coin THEN add 1 point.'

[text] Every program has INPUT (a key press, a click), PROCESS (the steps) and OUTPUT (what you see or hear).

[text] Ask: Who wrote it? Do they have evidence? When was it written? Does it make me feel very angry or excited? Strong feelings can be a warning sign.

column2: Digital Footprints and How AI Works
column5:
b3-dig-4: Understands digital footprint: posts can last forever
b3-dig-5: Knows how AI chatbots work at a simple level and why they can be wrong
column9:
[text] Your DIGITAL FOOTPRINT is the trail you leave online: posts, photos, comments, searches. It can last a very long time, even if you delete something.

[text] Before posting, ask: Would I be OK with my teacher, family or a future employer seeing this?

[text] AI chatbots learn patterns from huge amounts of text, then predict likely next words. They don't 'know' things like people do.

[text] That's why AI can sound confident but still be WRONG. This is sometimes called 'hallucinating'. Always check important facts.

b3-dig-2: Recognises scams, fake prizes and suspicious links
b3-dig-1: Creates strong passwords and never shares them
column9:
[text] A scam is a trick to get your money, your passwords or your personal information.

[text] Warning signs: 'You WON a prize!', 'Hurry, only 5 minutes left!', 'Click this link to claim', or messages asking for passwords or codes.

[text] Scammers use excitement or fear to make you act fast without thinking.

[text] The rule: STOP, don't click, and show a trusted adult.

[fact] Real companies will never ask for your password in a message.

[tryit] With a grown-up, look at a spam folder together (don't click anything!). Can you spot the warning signs?

column5:
b3-health-4: Understands stress and healthy ways to cope
b3-health-3: Friendship skills, dealing with bullying, asking for help
column9:
[text] Everyone feels stressed, worried or angry sometimes. Feelings aren't bad. They're signals from your body and brain.

[text] Stress can show up in your body: a fast heartbeat, a tummy ache, tight shoulders or trouble sleeping.

[text] Calm-down tools: slow breathing (in for 4, out for 6), moving your body, drawing or writing, going somewhere quiet, or a hug.

[text] Talking helps! Tell a parent, teacher or friend what's on your mind. Big problems feel smaller when you share them.

[fact] Breathing out slowly helps your body calm down.

[text] If worries don't go away, or you ever feel unsafe, tell a trusted adult. Getting help is brave, not weak.

[tryit] Try 'box breathing': breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4, hold for 4. Do it 4 times. How do you feel?

column5: b3-health-2: Basic first aid: cuts, burns, calling emergency services
column9:
[text] First aid is the help you give before a doctor arrives. Always get an adult first if you can.

[text] Small CUT: wash hands, clean with clean water, press gently with a clean cloth to stop bleeding, cover with a plaster.

[text] BURN: cool it under cool (not icy) running water for 20 minutes. Don't use butter or ice. Tell an adult.

[text] SERIOUS emergency: call your local emergency number, say where you are and what happened, and follow instructions.

column9:
[text] Food labels show what's inside: energy (calories), fat, sugar, salt and more, usually per 100 g and per portion.

[text] Ingredients are listed from MOST to LEAST. If sugar is first, there's more sugar than anything else!

[text] Some countries use traffic-light colours: green = low, amber = medium, red = high.

column5: b3-health-5: Puberty: body changes and why they happen
column9:
[text] Puberty is when your body starts changing from a child's body into an adult's. It usually starts somewhere between about 8 and 14. Everyone's timing is different, and that's normal.

[text] Common changes for everyone: growth spurts, new body hair, more sweat (time for deodorant and daily washing), spots, and stronger feelings or mood changes.

[text] Many girls develop breasts and start having periods. Many boys' voices get deeper and their shoulders get broader.

[text] Questions are normal! Ask a parent, school nurse or another trusted adult. Reliable health websites can help too.

column9:

[text] Compare: PURPOSE (to inform, entertain or persuade?), POINT OF VIEW (who is telling it?), and FACTS vs FEELINGS.

[text] Use words like 'Both…', 'However…', 'In contrast…' to compare.

[text] VERBS are action or being words: run, think, is.

[text] ADJECTIVES describe nouns: a TALL tree. ADVERBS describe verbs, often ending in -ly: she ran QUICKLY.

[text] TENSE shows time: I walk (present), I walked (past), I will walk (future).

b3-lang-1: Reads texts of a few paragraphs independently and finds the main idea and supporting details (GPF G4–6)
b3-lang-2: Makes inferences: works out what is not said directly
column9:
[text] The MAIN IDEA is what a paragraph is mostly about. The other sentences are DETAILS that support it.

[text] The main idea is often in the first sentence (the topic sentence), but not always. Sometimes it's at the end, or not written at all.

[text] Test: ask 'What is this mostly about?' Then check: do most sentences support your answer?

[fact] Example: 'Octopuses are amazing escape artists. They can squeeze through tiny gaps. They change colour to hide. Some even squirt ink.' Main idea: octopuses are good at escaping. Everything else is a detail.

[text] An INFERENCE is working out something the writer doesn't say directly, using clues in the text.

[tryit] Pick a paragraph from any book. Write its main idea in 10 words or fewer.

[text] Start with a TOPIC SENTENCE that says the main idea. Add 2–4 SUPPORTING sentences with details or examples. End with a CONCLUDING sentence.

[text] Good writers PLAN (list ideas), DRAFT (write it), then EDIT (fix spelling, punctuation and unclear bits).

[text] PERIMETER is the distance all the way around a shape. Add up all the sides.

[text] AREA is the space inside. For a rectangle: length × width. It's measured in square units (cm²).

[text] A right angle is 90° (like a square corner). Acute angles are smaller than 90°; obtuse angles are between 90° and 180°.

[fact] The angles inside any triangle always add up to 180°.

column5: b3-math-2: Understands, compares and adds fractions; links fractions, decimals and percentages
column9:
[text] A fraction like 3/4 means 3 parts out of 4 equal parts. The bottom number (denominator) says how many parts the whole is cut into.

[text] Same denominator? Just compare the tops. 5/8 is bigger than 3/8 because 5 pieces is more than 3 pieces of the same size.

[text] Same numerator? The SMALLER denominator wins! 1/3 is bigger than 1/5, because a pizza cut into 3 has bigger slices than one cut into 5.

[text] Different tops and bottoms? Make the denominators the same. For 2/3 and 3/4, use twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. So 3/4 is bigger.

[tryit] Fold two paper strips the same length. Fold one into 3 parts and one into 4. Shade 2/3 and 3/4 and compare.

column9:
[text] A BAR CHART compares amounts. A LINE GRAPH shows change over time, like temperature through the day.

[text] Always read the title, the labels on each axis and the scale.

[text] The MEAN (average) = add all the values, then divide by how many there are.

[fact] Example: scores 4, 6 and 8. Sum = 18, and 18 ÷ 3 = 6. The mean is 6.

column5: b3-math-5: Solves multi-step word problems and checks if the answer is reasonable
column9:
[text] Read the problem twice. Underline the numbers and the question.

[text] Decide the steps: what do you need to find first?

[text] ESTIMATE first, then check that your answer is reasonable. If you estimated about 100 and got 1,000, check again!

[fact] Example: 3 packs of 12 eggs, 5 broken. Step 1: 3 × 12 = 36. Step 2: 36 − 5 = 31. Estimate: about 35, so 31 is reasonable.

[text] Division is the opposite of multiplication: if 6 × 7 = 42, then 42 ÷ 7 = 6.

[text] For big multiplication, split numbers: 23 × 4 = (20 × 4) + (3 × 4) = 80 + 12 = 92.

[fact] Trick for 9s: 9 × 7 = 63, and 6 + 3 = 9. The digits of the 9 times table (up to 9 × 10) always add to 9!

b3-money-3: Compares prices and value for money
column9:
[text] A BUDGET is a plan for your money. It shows money coming in (income) and money going out (spending).

[text] A simple plan: split money into Save, Spend and Share (giving to others or charity).

[text] Example: you get 50 coins. Save 20, spend 25, share 5. Total = 50. A budget must add up!

[text] Comparing prices helps your money go further. Bigger isn't always cheaper. Work out the cost of each item.

[fact] Many adults use the same idea, with more categories like rent, food and travel.

[text] WEATHER is what happens day to day. CLIMATE is the usual pattern over many years.

[text] Gases like carbon dioxide trap heat around the Earth like a blanket. This is the greenhouse effect, and it keeps Earth warm enough to live on.

[text] Burning coal, oil and gas adds extra carbon dioxide, so the Earth is warming. Scientists agree this is mainly caused by human activity.

[text] Solutions include clean energy (sun, wind, water), saving energy, protecting forests and wasting less.

[text] PRODUCERS (plants) make food from sunlight. CONSUMERS eat other living things. DECOMPOSERS (fungi, bacteria) break down dead things.

[text] An ECOSYSTEM is all the living things in an area plus their environment, all depending on each other.

[fact] If one part of a food chain disappears, the others are affected. Fewer rabbits can mean fewer foxes.

[text] GRAVITY pulls things towards Earth. FRICTION slows things when surfaces rub. MAGNETS attract some metals, like iron.

[text] SIMPLE MACHINES make work easier: levers, pulleys, ramps, wheels and axles.

[text] Decide what you MEASURE, then record results in a table.

[text] Repeat the test to make sure results are reliable, then write a CONCLUSION: what did you find out?

column5: b3-sci-4: Knows the water cycle and the solar system
column9:
[text] The water you drink today may once have been in an ocean, a cloud or a glacier. Earth keeps reusing its water in a loop called the water cycle.

[text] 1. Evaporation: the Sun heats water in oceans, lakes and rivers. It turns into water vapour, a gas, and rises.

[text] 2. Condensation: high up, the air is cooler. The vapour cools into tiny droplets that form clouds.

[text] 3. Precipitation: droplets join and get heavy. They fall as rain, snow, sleet or hail.

[text] 4. Collection: water gathers in oceans, rivers, lakes and underground. Then the cycle starts again.

[tryit] Breathe on a cold mirror or window. The foggy patch is condensation: water vapour from your breath turning into droplets.

[text] Example: 'Plan a class party' becomes: pick a date, make a guest list, choose food, plan games, clean up.

[text] Each small step is easier to solve. Then you put the pieces together.

[text] In math word problems: 1) What do I know? 2) What am I asked? 3) What steps get me there? 4) Does my answer make sense?

[text] Mesopotamia (Tigris and Euphrates, modern Iraq) gave us one of the first writing systems, cuneiform, around 5,000 years ago.

column2: Festivals of Light Around the World
column5: b3-world-5: Beliefs and practices of world religions and non-religious worldviews, compared respectfully
column9:
[text] Many religions and cultures have festivals that use light. Here are three. People of each faith celebrate in their own ways, and not everyone celebrates.

[text] Diwali is celebrated by many Hindus, Sikhs and Jains, mostly in October or November. People light small oil lamps called diyas, and many see it as celebrating light over darkness and good over evil.

[text] Hanukkah is a Jewish festival lasting eight nights. Families light candles on a special candle holder, adding one more each night. It remembers the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem long ago.

[text] Christmas is when Christians celebrate the birth of Jesus. Many people decorate with lights and candles. Some people celebrate Christmas as a cultural holiday too.

[tryit] Ask your family: do you have a festival you celebrate? What do you do on that day?

[text] LONGITUDE lines run north–south from pole to pole. The Prime Meridian (0°) passes through Greenwich, London.

[text] Places near the equator are usually hot (tropical). Near the poles it's cold (polar). In between is temperate.

column2: Art Movements and Your Own Project
column5:
b4-arts-1: Art movements and how art reflects its time and place
b4-arts-3: Creates a project in a chosen medium (drawing, music, film, design)
column9:
[text] Art reflects its time and place. IMPRESSIONISM (1870s France) captured light and moments with quick brushstrokes. CUBISM (early 1900s) showed objects from several angles at once.

[text] Around the world: Mughal miniature painting (India), Ukiyo-e prints (Japan), the Harlem Renaissance (USA, 1920s) and Mexican muralism (1920s) all responded to their societies.

[text] Your project: choose a medium (drawing, music, film, design), set a goal, make drafts, ask for feedback, and improve. Share your process, not just the final piece.

column5: b4-arts-2: Music: scales, chords, melody and harmony basics
column9:
[text] A SCALE is a set of notes in order, going up or down. The C major scale uses only the white keys on a piano: C D E F G A B C.

[text] MELODY is a sequence of single notes, the part you can hum. HARMONY is notes played at the same time to support the melody.

[text] A CHORD is three or more notes played together. The most common is a triad: the 1st, 3rd and 5th notes of a scale.

[text] C major chord = C, E and G (notes 1, 3 and 5 of the C major scale). Major chords often sound bright; minor chords often sound sadder.

[fact] Many popular songs use just four chords, repeated in different patterns.

column5: b4-comp-3: Binary numbers and how computers store data
column9:
[text] Computers store everything (numbers, text, photos, music) using just two digits: 0 and 1. This is BINARY.

[text] Each 0 or 1 is a BIT. 8 bits make a BYTE.

[text] In our normal (decimal) system, columns are worth 1, 10, 100… In binary, columns are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… (each double the last).

[text] Binary 1011 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. Add up the column values where there's a 1.

[fact] With 8 bits you can make 256 different patterns (0 to 255). That's why many old games had limits of 255!

[text] AI can generate text, images and code, but it can be confidently wrong and it doesn't understand like a human.

column5: b4-dig-4: Cyberbullying: how to respond, report and support others
column9:
[text] Cyberbullying is repeated, deliberate online cruelty: mean messages, sharing embarrassing photos, excluding someone, or impersonation.

[text] If it happens to you: don't reply in anger. Screenshot evidence, block, report on the platform, and tell a trusted adult.

[text] If you see it: don't like or share. Privately check on the person ('Are you OK?') and report it. Bystanders can make a big difference.

b4-dig-3: Healthy social media habits and recognising addictive design

[text] Building an app costs money: developers, servers, designers. So when an app is free, it makes money some other way.

[text] Ads: the app shows you adverts. Advertisers pay more when they can target people precisely, so many apps collect data about what you like, where you are and who you talk to.

[text] In-app purchases: the app is free to start, but extra lives, skins or features cost money (often called 'freemium').

[text] Your attention: the longer you stay, the more ads you see. That's why some apps use endless scrolling, autoplay and streaks. These designs are built to keep you hooked.

[fact] Honest Learn is funded by donations. We show no ads and never sell your data.

[tryit] Pick an app you use. Look at its privacy settings. What data does it collect? Can you turn some of it off?

[text] DEEPFAKES are AI-made videos, images or audio that make it look like someone said or did something they didn't.

[text] Pause before sharing, especially if it makes you angry or shocked. Emotions spread fakes fastest.

column5: b4-health-1: Mental health: anxiety, mood, self-esteem, where to get help
column9:
[text] Mental health is how we think, feel and cope. Everyone has mental health, just like physical health. It goes up and down.

[text] Anxiety (worry), low mood and stress are common, especially during the teenage years. Signs to take seriously: feelings that last weeks, stop you doing normal things, or change sleep and appetite.

[text] Things that help: sleep, exercise, time outdoors, talking to people you trust, limiting doom-scrolling, and being kind to yourself.

[text] Getting help is a strength. Talk to a parent, teacher, school counsellor or doctor. If you ever feel unsafe, contact your local emergency number or a youth helpline straight away.

column5: b4-health-3: Peer pressure, healthy friendships and consent in everyday life
column9:
[text] Peer pressure is feeling pushed to do something to fit in. It can be positive (joining a study group) or negative (risky dares, being unkind to someone).

[text] Healthy friends respect your 'no', support you, and don't make you feel bad for being yourself.

[text] CONSENT in everyday life means asking and respecting the answer: before borrowing things, sharing someone's photo, or hugging. Consent can be changed at any time.

[text] Saying no: be clear and short ('No thanks'), suggest something else, or leave. Real friends will accept it.

column5: b4-health-5: Puberty, reproduction and relationships education
column9:
[text] Puberty is driven by hormones (mainly oestrogen and testosterone). These cause growth, body changes and the ability to reproduce.

[text] Human reproduction: a sperm cell from a male joins an egg cell from a female (fertilisation). The fertilised egg can grow into a baby in the uterus over about 9 months.

[text] The menstrual cycle (periods) is about monthly and is a normal sign that the body is preparing for possible pregnancy.

[text] Healthy relationships of any kind are built on respect, trust, honesty and consent. Nobody should pressure you to do anything you're not ready for.

[text] Questions are normal. Trusted adults, school nurses, doctors and reliable health websites can help.

column5: b4-health-2: Nutrition, exercise and sleep for teenagers
column9:
[text] While you sleep, your brain stores what you learned that day, your body repairs itself, and you grow.

[text] Sleep experts recommend 9–12 hours a night for ages 6–12, and 8–10 hours for teenagers. Many teens get much less.

[text] Too little sleep can make it harder to focus, remember things and control your mood. It can also affect your health.

[text] Teen body clocks naturally shift later, so feeling awake at night is normal. Good habits help: a regular bedtime, a dark, cool room, and no screens for 30–60 minutes before bed.

[fact] Bright screens late at night can make it harder to fall asleep. Notifications keep your brain alert too.

[tryit] Keep a sleep diary for a week: bedtime, wake time and how you feel. Do you see a pattern?

[text] Vapes are not harmless: they can contain nicotine and other chemicals, and many are marketed with sweet flavours to attract young people.

[text] Alcohol and other drugs can affect judgement, memory, mental health and safety, and many are illegal for young people.

[text] If you're worried about yourself or a friend, talk to a trusted adult or health professional. In an emergency, call your local emergency number.

column5: b4-lang-3: Understands figurative language: metaphor, simile, irony
column9:
[text] Figurative language means words that go beyond their literal meaning to create images or feelings.

[text] A SIMILE compares two things using 'like' or 'as': 'Her voice was as smooth as honey.'

[text] A METAPHOR says one thing IS another: 'Time is a thief.' (Time doesn't steal, but it takes moments from us.)

[text] IRONY is when the opposite of what's expected happens or is meant. A fire station burning down is situational irony. Saying 'Great weather!' in a storm is verbal irony.

[text] Personification gives human qualities to non-human things: 'The wind whispered through the trees.'

[text] An equation is a balance: both sides are equal. To find the unknown (x), do the same thing to both sides until x is alone.

[text] Undo operations in reverse order. In 3x + 4 = 19, x was multiplied by 3 and then 4 was added. So first subtract 4, then divide by 3.

[text] 3x + 4 = 19 → 3x = 15 → x = 5. Check: 3 × 5 + 4 = 19 ✓

[fact] Always check your answer by putting it back into the original equation.

column5: b4-money-3: How businesses work: cost, price, profit
column9:
[text] Businesses have COSTS: materials, wages, rent, energy. They set a PRICE for their product.

[text] PROFIT = revenue (money from sales) − costs. If costs are bigger, the business makes a LOSS.

[text] Price too high and fewer people buy; too low and you may not cover costs. Businesses also compete with each other.

[fact] Example: lemonade costs 0.30 per cup to make and sells for 1.00. Selling 50 cups: revenue 50, costs 15, profit 35.

b4-money-1: Budgeting, saving and simple vs compound interest
b4-money-2: Debt, loans and why 'buy now, pay later' can be risky
column9:
[text] INTEREST is money paid for using money. Banks may pay you interest on savings, and you pay interest when you borrow.

[text] SIMPLE interest is paid only on the original amount. 1,000 at 10% simple interest earns 100 every year.

[text] COMPOUND interest is paid on the original amount AND on interest already earned. 1,000 at 10%: year 1 → 1,100; year 2 → 1,210; year 3 → 1,331.

[text] Compounding helps savers grow money over time. But it also makes debts grow fast if you don't pay them off!

[fact] Rule of 72: divide 72 by the interest rate to estimate how many years it takes money to double. At 6%, about 12 years.

column5: b4-sci-2: Atoms, elements, compounds, the periodic table; chemical vs physical change
column9:
[text] Everything is made of tiny particles called ATOMS. An atom has a nucleus (protons and neutrons) with electrons around it.

[text] An ELEMENT is a substance made of only one kind of atom, like oxygen (O), gold (Au) or carbon (C). The periodic table lists all 118 known elements.

[text] A COMPOUND forms when atoms of two or more DIFFERENT elements are chemically bonded together. Water (H₂O) is 2 hydrogen atoms bonded to 1 oxygen atom.

[text] A compound can be very different from its elements. Sodium is a reactive metal and chlorine is a poisonous gas, but together they make table salt (NaCl).

[text] A MIXTURE is different: substances are mixed but not chemically bonded, like sand and water. You can often separate them by filtering.

[fact] Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe.

[text] The nucleus holds DNA, which is organised into GENES: instructions for building and running the body. Offspring inherit genes from their parents.

[text] EVOLUTION by NATURAL SELECTION: individuals vary; those with traits better suited to their environment tend to survive and reproduce more, so those traits become more common over many generations.

[text] Scientists CLASSIFY living things into groups (kingdom → species) based on shared features and DNA.

[text] The ROCK CYCLE: IGNEOUS rocks form from cooled magma, SEDIMENTARY from layers of sediment, METAMORPHIC from rocks changed by heat and pressure.

[text] Energy can't be created or destroyed. It changes form: chemical → kinetic (movement) → thermal (heat), and so on.

[text] A CIRCUIT needs a complete loop, an energy source (cell/battery) and components (bulbs, motors).

[text] SERIES circuit: one loop. If one bulb breaks, all go out. PARALLEL circuit: several branches. Others stay on if one breaks.

[text] A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning. It can make an argument sound convincing when it isn't. Spotting them protects you from being manipulated by ads, social media and even friends.

[text] Bandwagon: 'Everyone's doing it, so it must be right.' Popularity doesn't prove something is true or good.

[text] Straw man: twisting someone's argument into a weaker version, then attacking that. 'You want less homework? So you think school is pointless?'

[text] False choice: pretending there are only two options when there are more. 'Either you're with us or against us.'

[text] Attacking the person: criticising the speaker instead of their argument. 'Why listen to her about climate? She's only 14.'

column5: b4-world-5: Colonialism, independence movements and world wars — multiple perspectives
column9:
[text] From the 1500s to the 1900s, several European powers (and others, like Japan) built EMPIRES by taking control of lands in Africa, Asia, the Americas and Oceania.

[text] Colonisers often took resources and land, and imposed their rule on local people. Effects included exploitation, famines, and borders drawn without local consent. Historians also debate long-term effects on infrastructure, languages and institutions.

[text] INDEPENDENCE movements, especially after 1945, led to many new nations: India and Pakistan (1947), Ghana (1957), Algeria (1962) and many more. Some were peaceful mass movements; others involved war.

[text] World War I (1914–1918) and World War II (1939–1945) killed tens of millions of people worldwide, including the Holocaust, in which Nazi Germany murdered six million Jews and millions of others. After WWII, the United Nations was founded (1945) to try to prevent future wars.

[text] People in different countries remember these events differently. Reading sources from several perspectives is essential.

column5: b4-world-4: Types of government and how laws are made
column9:
[text] Countries are governed in different ways. In a DEMOCRACY, citizens elect leaders. In a MONARCHY, a king or queen is head of state (often with an elected parliament too). In an AUTHORITARIAN system, power is held by one leader or party with limited elections or freedoms.

[text] Many countries separate power into 3 branches: LEGISLATIVE (makes laws, such as a parliament), EXECUTIVE (runs the country, such as a president or prime minister) and JUDICIAL (courts that interpret laws).

[text] Laws are usually proposed, debated, voted on, and then signed into law. Courts can check laws against a constitution.

[text] People disagree about which policies are best. That's normal in a democracy. Look at the evidence and listen to different views.

[text] Historians ask WHY things happened (causes) and WHAT changed afterwards (consequences). Most events have several causes: long-term and short-term.

[text] Example: the printing press (Gutenberg, around 1440, building on earlier Chinese and Korean printing) made books cheaper. Consequences: more people could read, and ideas spread faster.

[text] Example: the Industrial Revolution (from the late 1700s, starting in Britain) brought factories and railways, and moved people to cities. It also brought child labour and pollution, which led to new laws.

[text] World history happens everywhere at once. The Mali Empire, the Mughal Empire and Ming China were all powerful while Europe changed too.

column5: b4-world-2: Population, migration, cities, resources and trade
column9:
[text] Migration means people moving from one place to live in another, within a country or to another country. Humans have migrated throughout history.

[text] PUSH factors make people want to leave a place: few jobs, conflict, natural disasters, or lack of schools or healthcare.

[text] PULL factors attract people to a new place: jobs, safety, family already there, education or a better climate.

[text] URBANISATION is people moving from the countryside to cities. Today more than half of the world's people live in cities.

[text] Migration affects both places: new skills, cultures and foods arrive, and communities also have to adapt. People have different views about migration policy, and it's worth understanding the evidence behind each view.

column5: b5-arts-3: Copyright, Creative Commons and fair use for creators
column9:
[text] COPYRIGHT automatically protects original creative work (writing, music, art, photos, code) the moment it's made. Only the owner can copy, share or adapt it, unless they give permission.

[text] PUBLIC DOMAIN works have no copyright, usually because it expired (often decades after the creator's death, depending on the country). Anyone can use them freely.

[text] CREATIVE COMMONS (CC) licences let creators give permission in advance. BY = credit the creator. SA = share your adaptation under the same licence. NC = non-commercial use only. ND = no changes allowed.

[text] Many countries allow limited use without permission for things like criticism, teaching or parody ('fair use' in the US, 'fair dealing' in the UK, India and others). The rules differ and are narrower than many people think.

[fact] Honest Learn writes its own lessons and lists sources. Wikipedia text is CC BY-SA, so anything adapted from it must credit Wikipedia and use the same licence.

[text] Re-reading notes and highlighting feel productive but are among the least effective ways to study.

[text] Active recall (the testing effect): close the book and pull information out of memory with flashcards, practice questions, or explaining it aloud. Retrieval strengthens memory more than re-reading does.

[text] Spaced repetition (the spacing effect): review material over increasing gaps (1 day, 3 days, a week) instead of cramming it all at once.

[text] Interleaving: mix different types of problems in one session, so you learn to choose the right method, not just repeat one.

column5: b5-comp-1: Programming with data structures, algorithms and problem solving
column9:
[text] LINEAR SEARCH checks items one by one. For a list of n items it may take up to n checks. Fine for small lists, slow for huge ones.

[text] BINARY SEARCH works on a SORTED list. Check the middle item. If the target is smaller, discard the right half. If bigger, discard the left half. Repeat.

[text] Each step halves the list, so 1,000,000 sorted items need at most about 20 checks (2²⁰ ≈ 1,000,000). Linear search could need a million.

[text] Computer scientists describe this with Big-O notation: linear search is O(n); binary search is O(log n).

[fact] You use binary search when you guess a number between 1 and 100 by always guessing the middle: at most 7 guesses.

column9:
[text] Most account hacks don't need genius hackers. They use reused passwords, phishing and missing two-factor authentication.

[text] Use a different strong password for every important account. A password manager can create and remember them. A long passphrase (4+ random words) is strong and memorable.

[text] TWO-FACTOR AUTHENTICATION (2FA) adds a second step: something you have (an app code or security key) on top of something you know (your password). Even if your password leaks, the attacker usually can't log in.

[text] PHISHING: fake messages that trick you into giving passwords or codes. Red flags: urgency, odd sender addresses, links to look-alike sites, requests for codes.

[text] NEVER share a 2FA code. No real company will ask you for one. Set up recovery options (backup codes, a recovery email) before you need them.

column5: b5-health-3: First aid and CPR basics
column9:
[text] This lesson is an introduction, not a certificate. Take a hands-on first-aid course (often free or cheap from Red Cross/Red Crescent and other groups). Practice is what makes you able to help.

[text] 1. DANGER: check the area is safe for you first. 2. RESPONSE: tap the shoulders and shout 'Are you OK?'. 3. Call your local EMERGENCY NUMBER (or get someone to) and put the phone on speaker.

[text] If the person is unresponsive and not breathing normally, start CPR. Push hard and fast in the centre of the chest (about 5–6 cm deep for an adult), 100–120 times a minute, letting the chest come back up between pushes.

[text] Hands-only CPR (compressions without rescue breaths) is recommended for untrained bystanders helping an adult who collapsed. Keep going until help or an AED (defibrillator) arrives.

[text] An AED gives spoken instructions. Turn it on and follow them. It only shocks if it detects a rhythm that needs it.

[text] If someone is unresponsive but breathing normally, put them in the recovery position (on their side) and keep checking their breathing until help arrives.

[text] Warning signs of an unhealthy or abusive relationship: controlling who you see, checking your phone, jealousy presented as 'love', threats, put-downs, or pressure to do things you don't want to.

column5: b5-lang-2: Writes research essays with citations and avoids plagiarism
column9:
[text] PLAGIARISM is presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own. In school and work it's taken seriously: failing an assignment, losing a job, or worse.

[text] Changing a few words (patchwriting) is still plagiarism if the ideas and structure are someone else's and you don't credit them.

[text] Avoid it by: putting exact words in quotation marks with a citation; paraphrasing in your own words AND citing the source; keeping a list of sources while you research.

[text] A citation tells readers where an idea came from (author, title, date, publisher or URL) so they can check it. Common styles are APA, MLA and Chicago.

[text] Using AI: if you use an AI tool to help, follow your school's rules and say how you used it. AI can also invent fake sources, so always check that a source really exists.

[fact] Common knowledge (e.g. 'Paris is the capital of France') usually doesn't need a citation. Statistics and specific claims do.

column9:
[text] Structure: open with a hook (question, story or surprising fact), state your main point, give 2–3 supporting points with evidence, and end with a strong conclusion.

[text] Delivery: speak slower than feels natural, pause after key points, make eye contact, and use notes with key words, not a full script.

[text] Nerves are normal. Most speakers feel them. Practise out loud, breathe slowly, and focus on your message, not yourself.

column9:
[text] Aristotle described three appeals: ETHOS (credibility: 'As a doctor…'), PATHOS (emotion: stories, vivid images) and LOGOS (logic: evidence, statistics, reasoning).

[text] Other devices: rhetorical questions, repetition ('We shall fight… we shall fight…'), the rule of three, and contrast.

[text] Critical reading asks: What is the writer trying to make me feel or do? Which appeals are strongest? What's left out?

column5: b5-math-3: Statistics: distributions, sampling, correlation vs causation
column9:
[text] Two things are correlated when they tend to change together. That doesn't mean one causes the other.

[text] Confounding variable: a third factor causing both. Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. Ice cream doesn't cause drowning. Hot weather increases both swimming and ice-cream buying.

[text] Reverse causation: maybe B causes A, not A causes B. People who exercise more may sleep better, or people who sleep better may have more energy to exercise.

[text] Coincidence: with enough data, some unrelated things will line up by chance.

[text] How scientists test causation: randomised controlled trials. People are randomly assigned to groups so the only systematic difference is the thing being tested.

[tryit] Find a news headline that says 'X linked to Y'. List one possible confounder and one possible reverse-causation story.

column2: Real-Life Money Maths: Loans, Inflation, Percentages
column5: b5-math-5: Financial maths: loans, inflation, percentages in real life
column9:
[text] INFLATION means prices rise over time, so money buys less. With 5% inflation, something costing 100 costs about 105 next year.

[text] Loans charge interest. The APR (annual percentage rate) includes fees, so it's the fairest number to compare loans by.

[text] Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. A price going from 80 to 100 is a 25% increase.

[fact] Minimum payments on a credit card can make a debt last years and cost far more than the original amount.

column5: b5-math-1: Quadratics, functions, exponents and logarithms
column9:
[text] A QUADRATIC has an x² term, like y = x² − 5x + 6. Its graph is a U-shaped parabola. Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0 by factorising: (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0, so x = 2 or x = 3.

[text] EXPONENTS: 2⁵ = 32. Rules: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, and (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ.

[text] A LOGARITHM asks 'what power?': log₂(32) = 5 because 2⁵ = 32. Logs turn multiplication into addition and appear in sound (decibels), earthquakes and pH.

column2: Intro to Calculus: Rates of Change
column5: b5-math-4: Introduction to calculus ideas (rates of change)
column9:
[text] Calculus studies change. The GRADIENT of a curve at a point tells you how fast something is changing right then, like speed from a distance–time graph.

[text] The DERIVATIVE gives that rate. For y = xⁿ, the derivative is nxⁿ⁻¹. So y = x² has derivative 2x, and at x = 3 the slope is 6.

[text] Calculus is used in physics, economics, medicine (drug doses), engineering and machine learning.

column5: b5-money-1: Opening a bank account, budgeting a monthly income
column9:
[text] A CURRENT/CHECKING account is for everyday spending (with a debit card). A SAVINGS account earns interest for money you don't need now.

[text] Check fees, minimum balances and interest rates. Keep your PIN and online banking details private.

[text] The 50/30/20 guideline: about 50% needs (rent, food, transport), 30% wants, 20% savings or paying off debt. Adjust it to your situation.

[text] Build an EMERGENCY FUND: a few months of essential costs, for surprises like losing a job or a repair.

column2: Credit, Credit Scores and Student Finance
column5: b5-money-2: Credit, credit scores, loans and student finance
column9:
[text] CREDIT is borrowing money to pay back later, with interest. Credit cards, loans and 'buy now, pay later' are all credit.

[text] A CREDIT SCORE (in many countries) estimates how reliably you repay. Paying on time and not borrowing too much helps; missed payments hurt.

[text] Student finance differs hugely by country: grants (don't repay), scholarships, and loans (with different interest and repayment rules). Read the terms carefully.

[text] Avoid high-cost loans (like payday loans) and loan apps that ask for access to your contacts or photos. These are red flags.

column5: b5-money-4: Investing basics: risk, diversification, avoiding scams
column9:
[text] Every real investment has risk. In general, higher possible returns come with higher risk of losing money. Anyone promising high returns with 'no risk' is a red flag.

[text] Ponzi scheme: early investors are paid with money from new investors, not real profits. It collapses when new money stops coming in.

[text] Pump-and-dump: promoters hype a cheap stock or coin on social media, the price jumps, they sell, and everyone else is left with losses.

[text] Other red flags: pressure to act now, 'secret' strategies, payments only in crypto or gift cards, and unregistered sellers.

[fact] Many countries have an official register of licensed investment firms. Check it before investing.

column5: b5-sci-2: Chemistry: bonding, reactions, acids/bases, moles basics
column9:
[text] IONIC bonds form when electrons transfer (Na⁺Cl⁻ in salt). COVALENT bonds form when atoms share electrons (H₂O).

[text] In a reaction, atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed, so equations must balance: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

[text] The pH scale runs from 0 (strongly acidic) to 14 (strongly basic/alkaline). 7 is neutral (pure water). Acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation).

[text] A MOLE is a counting unit for particles: about 6.02 × 10²³ of them, just like a 'dozen' means 12.

[text] DNA is a double helix made of four bases (A, T, C, G). A always pairs with T, and C with G. The sequence of bases codes for proteins.

[text] You inherit one copy of each gene from each parent. Versions of genes are called ALLELES. A DOMINANT allele shows its effect even with just one copy; a RECESSIVE one needs two copies.

[text] ECOLOGY studies how organisms interact with each other and their environment: food webs, competition and nutrient cycles.

column2: How to Judge a Scientific Study
column5: b5-sci-4: Reads a scientific study and judges its quality (sample size, controls, peer review)
column9:
[text] Questions to ask: How big was the sample? Was there a CONTROL group? Were participants randomly assigned? Was it BLINDED (people didn't know who got what)?

[text] Was it PEER-REVIEWED (checked by other experts)? Who funded it? Has it been REPLICATED by other teams?

[text] One study is rarely the final word. Systematic reviews, which combine many studies, are stronger evidence.

[fact] Headlines often say 'X causes Y' when the study only found a correlation, or was done in mice!

column5: b5-sci-3: Physics: motion, Newton's laws, waves, electricity, energy
column9:
[text] FIRST LAW (inertia): an object stays at rest, or keeps moving at a constant velocity, unless a net (unbalanced) force acts on it. That's why you lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly.

[text] SECOND LAW: net force = mass × acceleration (F = ma). The same push accelerates a light object more than a heavy one. Force is measured in newtons (N).

[text] THIRD LAW: for every action force there is an equal and opposite reaction force. When you push on a wall, the wall pushes back on you with the same force. Rockets push gas down, and the gas pushes the rocket up.

[text] The two forces in the third law act on DIFFERENT objects, which is why they don't cancel out.

[fact] Seatbelts work against the first law: they apply the force that stops your body when the car stops suddenly.

[tryit] Push a light box and a heavy box with the same effort. Which speeds up more? Which law explains it?
