column5:
b5-think-3: Understands cognitive biases (confirmation bias, anchoring)
b5-think-1: Evaluates arguments and evidence in news and research
column9:
[text] Cognitive biases are predictable shortcuts in thinking. They're usually helpful, but they can lead us to wrong conclusions. Everyone has them, including experts.

[text] CONFIRMATION BIAS: noticing and believing information that supports what we already think, and ignoring what doesn't.

[text] ANCHORING: relying too much on the first number we see. A 'was 200, now 99' price tag makes 99 feel cheap even if the item is worth 50.

[text] AVAILABILITY HEURISTIC: judging how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Plane crashes get huge news coverage, so flying feels riskier than driving, but per kilometre it's much safer.

[text] Defences: look for evidence AGAINST your view, ask 'what would change my mind?', check base rates and real data, and slow down on important decisions.

[tryit] Pick a belief you hold strongly. Find the best argument against it, written by someone who disagrees.

[text] Decision tools: PROS AND CONS lists, COST–BENEFIT analysis (put rough values on outcomes), and '10-10-10' (how will I feel in 10 minutes, 10 months, 10 years?).

[text] Think about second-order consequences: what happens after the first effect?

[text] Ethical dilemmas have no easy answer. The 'trolley problem' asks whether it's right to divert harm from five people to one. People reason differently depending on consequences, duties and character.

[text] Good ethical reasoning: identify who is affected, consider different principles, and be willing to explain and change your view.

[text] Citizens usually have rights (vote, free speech, fair trial) and responsibilities (follow laws, pay taxes, serve on juries in some countries). These vary by country.

[text] Elections work in different ways: first-past-the-post, proportional representation and others. Each has trade-offs.

[text] Evaluating political claims: Is there evidence? Is the statistic in context? What do independent fact-checkers say? What would the other side say?

[text] This lesson doesn't tell you what to think. Good citizens understand different views and decide with evidence.

column5:
b5-world-1: 20th–21st century world history and globalisation
b5-world-3: Global challenges: climate, inequality, health, technology
column9:
[text] Since 1945: the Cold War (USA vs USSR) shaped much of the world until 1991. Dozens of countries became independent. China, India and others grew rapidly.

[text] GLOBALISATION is the growing connection of economies, people and cultures through trade, travel and the internet. It has lifted many out of poverty but also brought job losses in some places, and spread problems quickly (like pandemics).

[text] Global challenges include climate change, inequality, pandemics and the impact of new technology like AI. In 2015, UN members agreed 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to tackle them by 2030.

column5: b5-world-5: Philosophy and ethics: major traditions and questions
column9:
[text] Philosophy asks big questions: What is right? What can we know? What makes a good life?

[text] Three major approaches to ethics: CONSEQUENTIALISM (judge actions by results, such as the greatest good for the greatest number), DEONTOLOGY (some duties and rules matter whatever the results, such as not lying), and VIRTUE ETHICS (be a person of good character: honest, brave, kind).

[text] Traditions worldwide add rich perspectives: Confucian ideas of harmony and respect, Buddhist ideas of compassion and non-harm, Ubuntu ('I am because we are') from southern Africa, and religious ethics in many faiths.

[text] Philosophy doesn't hand you answers; it helps you reason carefully and understand people who think differently.

column5: b5-world-2: Economics basics: supply and demand, inflation, trade
column9:
[text] DEMAND is how much of something people want to buy at different prices. Usually, when the price goes up, people buy less.

[text] SUPPLY is how much sellers want to sell at different prices. Usually, when the price goes up, sellers want to sell more.

[text] The market price tends to settle where the amount people want to buy matches the amount offered: the EQUILIBRIUM.

[text] If demand rises (a product goes viral) and supply stays the same, prices tend to rise. If supply rises (a huge harvest), prices tend to fall.

[text] Real markets are messier: governments set rules and taxes, some sellers have lots of power, and people don't always act 'rationally'. Economists debate how much these matter.

[tryit] Think of a product that suddenly became popular. What happened to its price and why?
